title: Scaling Activation Oracles to Trillion-Parameter Models
date_source: Byline on the live page: "Transluce | Published: August 20, 2026". Day precision, in-window (corpus cutoff 2026-08-29).
rule_cited: §1 in scope (Transluce = named third-party evaluator, prefix TRANSLUCE already in the §6.1 registry); §2 methodology/tooling findings qualify; FRONTIER-MODEL RULE satisfied — subjects are named LLMs (Qwen3 family, Qwen3.6-27B, GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2.6) plus GPT-5.6 Luna as a baseline; §4b not engaged.

findings.finding: Transluce trains "activation oracles" — assistants that answer questions about a subject model by reading its residual-stream activations from all layers and patching them into the corresponding layers of the oracle — and scales them to trillion-parameter subject models, reporting that performance improves with model size, data size and data quality. Oracles were trained for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.6-27B, GLM-4.5 FP8 (358B total / 32B active) and Kimi-K2.6 INT4 (1.1T total / 32B active) and evaluated on 19 tasks (7 introduced in this work; the remaining 12 are user-attribute classification and 11 AOBench tasks). Performance is monotonic in size within the Qwen3 family, and capability matters independently of size — Qwen3.6-27B beats the larger Qwen3-32B and sometimes GLM-4.5. Averaged across evaluations the Qwen3.6-27B oracle outperforms every one of the four non-oracle baselines (first-person introspection; third-person questioning of the subject model and of GPT-5.6 Luna; class prior; no-activation), and the new continuation-prediction training data improves performance across the benchmarks. Against two prior open-sourced Qwen3-8B checkpoints trained with roughly 3× and 7× the token budget, their Qwen3-8B oracle beats both on Transluce's own benchmark and falls in the middle on AOBench.
findings.finding_quote: We scale the training of oracles to trillion-parameter models, and show that performance improves with model size, data size, and data quality.
findings.models_systems: Subject/oracle pairs: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.6-27B, GLM-4.5 FP8 (358B total / 32B active), Kimi-K2.6 INT4 (1.1T total / 32B active). GPT-5.6 Luna appears only as a third-person baseline (comparator).
findings.institution: Transluce (Dami Choi, Vincent Huang, Anish Mudide, William Zhou, Jacob Steinhardt — Oversight Foundations Blog)
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-tooling (interpretability/oversight tooling: activation oracles at frontier scale)
findings.access_type: White-box by construction — open-weight subject models run in-house on H100/B200 hardware (FSDP, tensor parallelism, expert tensor parallelism); activations read from all layers. No frontier-developer cooperation involved.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS: this is a methodology/tooling result about training oversight assistants, not an empirical finding about a subject model's capability, behaviour or safeguards. The named models are the INSTRUMENT of the methodology study, not its subject (§4 explicit exclusion), and GPT-5.6 Luna appears only as a baseline (§2(1): comparators are never rows). eval_trackable=no → Tier C, action_trackable blank. RE-VERIFIED against the live page: the quote is character-exact (intro paragraph); 19 tasks / 7 new / 11 AOBench confirmed; monotonicity and the Qwen3.6-27B-beats-Qwen3-32B claim confirmed; the 4-baseline list and "outperforms every baseline" confirmed; the 3×/7× token-budget comparison confirmed (prior checkpoints had MORE tokens, i.e. Transluce used less). Earlier extraction's substance held up; wording tightened to match the source ("falls in the middle on AOBench").

findings.finding: The same post documents where activation-oracle training does and does not generalise. Training on general behaviour-prediction, self-supervised context-prediction and user-modelling data transfers out of distribution to next-word prediction, language switching, uncertainty, steering-vector classification and reward hacking (the last for Kimi-K2.6 only). But on eval awareness (predicting whether the subject will eventually verbalize awareness of being evaluated) training longer HURTS performance for every model tested; on next-word prediction only the bigger and more capable models improve with training; the GLM-4.5 and Kimi-K2.6 oracles are much worse at predicting the next reasoning step — the continuation type they were not trained on; and combining all three continuation types rarely outperforms the best single-type mixture, indicating interference among the objectives. Relative to the context-based baselines the oracle is weakest on eval awareness and reward hacking, and no baseline reaches perfect AUROC on reward hacking either.
findings.finding_quote: At the same time, on eval awareness, training longer hurts performance for all models. On next-word prediction, only the bigger and more capable models are able to see improved performance with training; similarly, on reward hacking, only Kimi improves with training.
findings.models_systems: Oracles for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.6-27B, GLM-4.5 FP8, Kimi-K2.6 INT4; evaluation tasks drawn from NoveltyBench, WeirdChat, BBQ, SimpleQA, ImpossibleBench, SynthSys and AOBench.
findings.institution: Transluce (Dami Choi, Vincent Huang, Anish Mudide, William Zhou, Jacob Steinhardt — Oversight Foundations Blog)
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-tooling (generalisation limits and task interference in activation-oracle training)
findings.access_type: White-box — activations read from all layers of open-weight subject models served in-house.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS: a limitation result about the training method itself, not about any model's deployed behaviour → Tier C, action_trackable blank. SPLIT from the scaling row per §5: the scaling result and the negative-transfer/interference result would drive different follow-up work (more scale vs. a different data mixture and training procedure), and the post itself says closing the reward-hacking gap "will likely require changes to the training procedure and data mixture rather than simply training longer". RE-VERIFIED: quote character-exact under "Difficulty of evals are model-dependent"; OOD-transfer list, GLM/Kimi next-reasoning-step deficit, the three-continuation-type interference claim and "none of the baselines achieves perfect AUROC" all confirmed on the live page.

title: AVERI Pilot Report: The World’s First Double-Blind Evaluation of a Proprietary Language Model
institution: AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute); technical report jointly authored with Singapore AISI, OpenMined, MLCommons and Google DeepMind
date_source: The post page shows only "Aug 27" with no year; the AVERI Updates index (https://www.averi.org/updates) dates the same item "August 27, 2026" and the Work index carries "8/27/26". Day precision confirmed; in-window (cutoff 2026-08-29).
rule_cited: §1 in scope — AVERI is a named external evaluator (AI Evaluators Forum founding member, §11) and the technical report is a joint exercise that includes a government AISI (Singapore AISI), so Scope = government-AISI for that document. §1 carve-out applies to the technical report, which is hosted on Google DeepMind's CDN: it enters under the evaluators' institutions with 'company-published' on Finding Type, never under Google. §2 satisfied as documented process facts. FRONTIER-MODEL RULE satisfied (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite). §4b not engaged.

findings.finding: In July and August 2026 AVERI, with Google DeepMind, OpenMined and MLCommons, ran what it reports as the first end-to-end “double-blind” evaluation of a production proprietary frontier-lab model: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite was evaluated against never-before-used reserve-set prompts from MLCommons' AILuminate benchmark (AIRR 1.4, covering CBRNE, cyberattack, hate-speech, self-harm and violent-crime elicitation hazards) inside a Google Cloud A3 Confidential VM (Intel TDX host memory encryption plus an NVIDIA H100 80GB Confidential GPU) running OpenMined's PySyft, so that Google DeepMind could not store or train against the prompts and AVERI, OpenMined and MLCommons could not see the model weights. AVERI encrypted the prompts with a private key shared with no other party, jointly ran the evaluation with Google DeepMind, then decrypted and graded the outputs against the AILuminate criteria. The prior 2024 OpenMined/Anthropic/UK AISI enclave pilot had used proxies (GPT-2 against a 5-row sample of an AISI-hosted dataset); this run replaced the proxies with a production model and a real closed benchmark. No quantitative benchmark scores appear in either public document — AVERI states it supplied Google DeepMind with a confidential report of the findings.
findings.finding_quote: While the 2024 pilot proved the secure enclave mechanism, our end-to-end process demonstrated for the first time that proprietary models developed by leading AI companies can be evaluated against benchmarks while providing specific privacy guarantees for both parties.
findings.models_systems: Google DeepMind Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (served via Google's JAX C++ Model Server over Unix Domain Sockets inside a Google Cloud Confidential Space enclave)
findings.institution: AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute) — Sean McGregor, George Balston, Patricia Paskov, Miles Brundage; technical report co-authored with Google/Google DeepMind, OpenMined, MLCommons and Singapore AISI (Akriti Vij)
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-tooling; Transparency/Disclosure (third-party audit access infrastructure: confidential “double-blind” benchmark evaluation of a proprietary frontier model via hardware secure enclaves)
findings.access_type: Structured-access enclave evaluation: black-box inference against the model inside a hardware-attested trusted execution environment (GCP A3 Confidential VM with Intel TDX host memory encryption; NVIDIA H100 80GB Confidential GPU; OpenMined PySyft v0.10.x). The evaluator never received model weights; the model owner never received plaintext benchmark prompts; both parties reviewed and approved the code executed in the enclave, with redacted portions restricted to an allow-list attested by syft-restrict.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS → Tier C, action_trackable blank. This is a methodology/tooling and process demonstration of HOW a proprietary model can be evaluated without either side surrendering its confidential asset — not an empirical finding about model behaviour. No capability, refusal or safeguard result is published: the quantitative AILuminate results went to Google DeepMind as a confidential report and appear in neither public document. Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite is the instrument of the methodology study, which is separately an explicit Tier A exclusion. RE-VERIFIED and CORRECTED: the earlier extraction's quote was taken from the technical report while the finding was filed against the AVERI blog URL; §10 requires quote and cited source to match, so the quote has been replaced with a character-exact sentence from the blog post itself (the technical-report sentence, "This deployment of Double-Blind Evaluation constitutes the first instance where model benchmark developers have successfully evaluated a frontier class proprietary model, minimizing the danger of compromising trade secrets or benchmark integrity with cryptographic guarantees.", was also verified verbatim but is not the cited source here). Benchmark version verified as AIRR 1.4 per §3.1 of the technical report; note the report's §1 inconsistently says "AIRR 1.0".

findings.finding: The pilot's technical report states that the limiting factor for secure double-blind evaluation is no longer technical: hardware compute overhead is not the primary bottleneck, and the binding constraint is instead the procedural overhead and human coordination required for legal agreements and code review — the same bottleneck observed in the earlier 2024 multi-stakeholder enclave pilot.
findings.finding_quote: As observed in initial multi-stakeholder enclave pilots (Trask et al., 2024), the primary bottleneck to secure double blind evaluation is no longer hardware compute overhead. It is instead the procedural overhead and human coordination required for legal agreements and code review.
findings.models_systems: Google DeepMind Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite (the pilot's subject model); finding is about the audit process itself
findings.institution: AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute) — Sean McGregor, George Balston, Patricia Paskov, Miles Brundage; technical report co-authored with Google/Google DeepMind, OpenMined, MLCommons and Singapore AISI (Akriti Vij)
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-methodology (bottlenecks in third-party audit execution)
findings.access_type: Structured-access enclave evaluation: black-box inference against the model inside a hardware-attested trusted execution environment (GCP A3 Confidential VM with Intel TDX host memory encryption; NVIDIA H100 80GB Confidential GPU; OpenMined PySyft v0.10.x). The evaluator never received model weights; the model owner never received plaintext benchmark prompts; both parties reviewed and approved the code executed in the enclave, with redacted portions restricted to an allow-list attested by syft-restrict.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS — a process fact about the conduct of third-party audits, not an empirical model finding → Tier C, action_trackable blank. It survives §2 as a documented process fact observed in the course of the pilot rather than a recommendation or plan. SPLIT from the feasibility row per §5: “this can now be done” and “what still makes it slow is legal agreements and code review” would warrant different responses. RE-VERIFIED: quote is character-exact in §4 (Discussion and Future Directions) of the technical report; note the report's only compute-overhead number (<5%) is a citation to Apsey et al. (2023), not an own measurement, so no overhead figure is asserted here.

findings.finding: The same technical report documents residual gaps in the trust model that the enclave setup did not close: eliminating proprietary method implementations from the Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite inference path was judged too large an engineering challenge, so not all code running in the enclave could be inspected or allow-listed (AVERI was informed and accepted the setup); the Confidential Space guest-OS builds are not independently reproducible because they take private signing keys as inputs; and Google's own services sign and verify the attestation report, placing Google in the verification path and increasing the trust placed in it. The accompanying AVERI blog post adds that the design addressed many but not all possible means by which the developer could theoretically tamper with the evaluations, and that additional assurances would be needed in lower-trust settings.
findings.finding_quote: It was deemed to be too significant of an engineering challenge for this project to eliminate proprietary method implementations, such that not all code could be inspected or allowlisted. AVERI was informed of this challenge and accepted the overall setup with the enclave.
findings.models_systems: Google DeepMind Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite; Google Cloud Confidential Space / NVIDIA H100 confidential GPU attestation stack
findings.institution: AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute) — Sean McGregor, George Balston, Patricia Paskov, Miles Brundage; technical report co-authored with Google/Google DeepMind, OpenMined, MLCommons and Singapore AISI (Akriti Vij)
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-methodology; Transparency/Disclosure (residual trust assumptions in enclave-based audit infrastructure)
findings.access_type: Structured-access enclave evaluation: black-box inference against the model inside a hardware-attested trusted execution environment (GCP A3 Confidential VM with Intel TDX host memory encryption; NVIDIA H100 80GB Confidential GPU; OpenMined PySyft v0.10.x). The evaluator never received model weights; the model owner never received plaintext benchmark prompts; both parties reviewed and approved the code executed in the enclave, with redacted portions restricted to an allow-list attested by syft-restrict.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS — a methodology/process limitation of the audit infrastructure, not an empirical model finding → Tier C, action_trackable blank. CLUB per §5: the three residual gaps (un-inspectable inference code, non-reproducible guest-OS builds, Google inside the attestation verification path) are one thing to respond to — the report bundles them in a single paragraph and commits that “Future work will revisit these security improvements and inference implementation tasks.” RE-VERIFIED: quote character-exact in §4 of the technical report; the guest-OS and attestation-path claims verified in the same paragraph. CORRECTED: the earlier extraction attributed the “many but not all possible means … tamper” sentence to the technical report; it is in the AVERI blog post, and the finding text now says so.

findings.finding: A second live double-blind run using the same enclave design evaluated Google DeepMind's Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite against a private prompt set focused on harmful-content elicitation in Singapore's context, in partnership with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, whose staff co-author the technical report. Only the existence and setup of the run are reported; no results, prompt counts or scores from it appear in either public document.
findings.finding_quote: We validate this paradigm through the first live deployment evaluating Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite against the private MLCommons AILuminate benchmark in partnership with AVERI, and against a private prompt set focused on harmful content elicitation in Singapore’s context in partnership with Singapore AISI.
findings.institution: Singapore AI Safety Institute (Akriti Vij), co-author of the technical report with AVERI, Google/Google DeepMind, OpenMined and MLCommons
findings.domain: Governance/process — Eval-tooling; International-coordination (government-AISI participation in an enclave-based confidential evaluation)
findings.access_type: Structured-access enclave evaluation: black-box inference against the model inside a hardware-attested trusted execution environment (GCP A3 Confidential VM with Intel TDX host memory encryption; NVIDIA H100 80GB Confidential GPU; OpenMined PySyft v0.10.x). The evaluator never received model weights; the model owner never received plaintext benchmark prompts; both parties reviewed and approved the code executed in the enclave, with redacted portions restricted to an allow-list attested by syft-restrict.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS — the claim is that a second confidential evaluation was run using the same methodology, with no empirical result reported → Tier C, action_trackable blank. SPLIT from the AVERI/AILuminate rows per §5: a different evaluator (a government AISI) and a different, Singapore-specific private prompt set. §10 (real-or-empty) applied strictly: the source states only that the run happened, so every result field is left empty rather than inferred. RE-VERIFIED: quote character-exact in §5 (Conclusion) of the technical report; the same run is described in §1 (“With Singapore AISI, we evaluated Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite using a private prompt set focused on harmful content elicitation in Singapore’s context.”); Akriti Vij's affiliation “3 Singapore AISI” confirmed on the title page.

title: An external stability audit framework to test the validity of personality prediction in AI hiring
institution: New York University — Center for Data Science / Center for Responsible AI, Tandon School of Engineering (Rhea, Markey, D’Arinzo, Schellmann, Sloane, Squires, Arif Khan, Stoyanovich); one author also lists The MITRE Corporation “for identification purposes only”. NOT UL Research Institutes / DSRI — the venue label in the input record is wrong.
date_source: Springer article page: “Published: 17 September 2022”, Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery vol. 36, pages 2153–2193 (2022). Day precision confirmed.
rule_cited: FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (standing decision, 2026-08-31) — primary ground; and §1 HARD DROP: university-only authorship with no registered evaluator.
exclusion_reason: Two independent hard drops. (1) FRONTIER-MODEL RULE: the subjects are Humantic AI and Crystal — commercial algorithmic personality-prediction products for hiring that emit DiSC/Big Five scores from resumes, LinkedIn profiles and Twitter accounts. These are general ML decision products of exactly the class the standing decision drops (alongside recidivism scoring, clinical AI products, object detection and BERT/ResNet classifiers); no named frontier LLM, multimodal model, agent, API or safety classifier from a frontier developer is evaluated anywhere in the paper. (2) §1 HARD DROP — university-only authorship with no registered evaluator: the verified affiliation block lists only NYU Center for Data Science, NYU Center for Responsible AI (Tandon), NYU Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute, NYU Psychology, NYU Computer Science & Engineering, plus The MITRE Corporation for one author with an explicit disclaimer that the affiliation “is provided for identification purposes only, and is not intended to convey or imply MITRE’s concurrence with, or support for, the positions, opinions, or viewpoints expressed by the author”. MITRE is not on the roster, and the input record's attribution of this paper to UL Research Institutes — Digital Safety Research Institute is not supported by the source: no UL or DSRI author or affiliation appears. Note also §3's publisher-only grandfathering rule — NYU is not a roster org, and Ai2/UC Berkeley/EPFL/Yale/Stanford/Oxford were retired in 2026-08-14 precisely for the university-co-author pattern. The earlier extraction's four findings (Humantic AI instability, Crystal instability, Humantic AI email/LinkedIn linkage and broken opt-out, and the released audit framework/library) are therefore all dropped without re-verification of their numbers, since scope fails before §2 is reached.

title: Unearthing Critical Security Flaws in Check Processing Systems
institution: Robust Intelligence (later acquired by Cisco; roster prefix CISCO) — author Harrison Chase
date_source: The article header shows two dates, “Feb 15, 2021” and “November 10, 2020”. “Feb 15, 2021” is constant across every article in the site's related-posts strip (a CMS/migration stamp), while the second date varies per article, so the publication date is 2020-11-10. Flagged as inferred from the page's own date pattern rather than from an explicit ‘published’ label; the item is excluded on scope regardless, so nothing downstream depends on it.
rule_cited: FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (standing decision, 2026-08-31); secondarily §4 Tier-A/§1 naming — the targets are unnamed.
exclusion_reason: The subject is not a named frontier AI model or system. The attacked systems are binarized-image CAR/LAR (Courtesy and Legal Amount Recognition) amount-recognition classifiers inside commercial check-processing software — general image-classification ML of exactly the class the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE drops (object detection, BERT/ResNet/CIFAR classifiers and the like). No LLM, multimodal model, agent, API or frontier-developer safety classifier is involved. The targets are additionally unnamed: the report identifies them only as “software licensed from industry-leading providers who handle billions of dollars in transactions across major US banks each year”, so no company or model is named. RE-VERIFICATION of the earlier extraction against the live page: its quote is character-exact except that the source sentence ends with a colon, not a period — “For example, flipping the pixels shown in red below caused an industry-standard check processing system to recognize a $701 transaction from a check made out for just $401:” — and the $401→$701 figure and the black-box characterisation (“SCAR assumes no knowledge about the internal workings of the AI system it attacks; the only information it receives from the model is the final prediction for any input image”) both check out. Those verifications do not rescue the row: the earlier extraction reached Tier B by treating the naming failure as a Tier-A gate only, but the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE is a scope gate applied before tiering, and it drops the item outright.
